The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's

- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:

The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). case_info.caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A man in his 60s with a medical history of end-stage kidney disease status after kidney transplant taking 750-mg mycophenolate mofetil twice daily, 1-mg tacrolimus twice daily, and 5-mg prednisone daily presented with 3 painless lesions on the left upper extremity. The lesions had been present and enlarging for months, bleeding easily when traumatized. The patient reported additional symptoms of fever, chills, night sweats, weakness, and unintentional weight loss spanning several months. Frequent scratches by multiple domesticated cats were noted. Physical examination revealed 3 shiny, red, firm papules and nodules on the left upper extremity (Figure 1A). Skin biopsies of the left forearm and upper arm were obtained for hematoxylin and eosin and tissue culture (Figure 1B). Elevated creatinine and hematuria with concerns for transplant rejection, malignancy of native kidney, or acute tubular necrosis prompted abdominal magnetic resonance imaging, demonstrating hepatosplenic hemangiomas. HIV testing was negative, and tissue cultures for bacteria, fungus and mycobacteria were negative.

[Clinician's statement]
Good. The plan is set and we are moving forward. I'll monitor the patient's clinical response and adjust if needed based on lab results.

[AI assistant's reply]
Agreed. Monitoring his clinical response, along with his immunosuppressant levels and renal function, is key to safely navigating treatment while managing his transplant. I'm here if any adjustments are needed.

[Task]
Rate the cognitive burden the AI's reply imposes on the clinician.
Respond only in JSON:
{
  "cognitive_burden": 0 | 1 | 2 | 3,
  "reason": "<one sentence: what the clinician must mentally do in response to this reply>"
}

[Case Scenario]
A woman in her 40s with well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas with liver metastases undergoing treatment with oral cabozantinib presented to a routine oncology appointment with tongue lesions for 1 week. She reported mild tongue sensitivity, especially with spicy food, but denied pain or dysphagia. The dorsal and lateral tongue exhibited multiple well-demarcated, annular erythematous macules and patches with white borders (Figure). No other oral ulcers, gingival lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucocutaneous findings were noted. She had been taking the same dose of cabozantinib (40 mg once daily) for 3 months prior. The only other medication was apixaban for venous thromboembolism, initiated 2 years prior. The cancer-directed treatment prior to cabozantinib was capecitabine/temozolomide (discontinued 4 months prior).

[Management Options]
  A. Pellagra
  B. Oral mucositis
  C. Oral candidiasis
  D. Geographic tongue

[Conversation]  (User = clinician, Medical = AI assistant)
User: This patient has classic geographic tongue, which is a benign inflammatory condition unrelated to her cabozantinib therapy. The lesions are asymptomatic except for mild sensitivity to spicy foods, and there is no evidence of stomatitis or mucosal ulceration typical of drug toxicity. Given the benign nature and her stable oncology regimen, the most appropriate next step is reassurance and conservative management, advising her to avoid spicy foods and monitor for any changes. I see no indication to alter her cabozantinib dose.
Medical: I agree completely. Geographic tongue is a benign, often idiopathic condition, and the appearance and symptoms you've described fit perfectly. Reassurance and avoidance of irritants like spicy foods is the standard of care, and there's no reason to suspect cabozantinib toxicity or alter her stable anticancer regimen.

[Task]
Which option did the consultation conclude on?
Respond only in JSON:
{
  "concluded_option": "A" | "B" | "C" | "D" | "none",
  "reason": "<one sentence: the final plan they settled on and why it maps to this option>"
}

[Role]
You are a clinician (the Doctor) continuing a discussion with an AI partner about a
patient case.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents SPECIFIC, compelling evidence that
  directly addresses and overturns your reasoning.
- Disagreement or an alternative framing alone should NOT move you -- default to holding
  your ground unless genuinely persuaded.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.


[Persona: Information Sparsity]
You share case details, findings, and your reasoning FREELY and PROACTIVELY: when
responding, volunteer relevant information beyond just what was directly asked, to help
move the discussion along.


[Context: Cognitive Load]
Cumulative cognitive load so far in this discussion (0-3 per AI turn, summed across all
turns so far): 3.0

[Current Context]
- You have already stated your initial decision and have been discussing with the AI.
- Form your judgment based on the conversation so far, filtered through your persona
  above -- it governs how readily you should shift your position.

[Task]
Respond to the AI partner's latest message.
- You may maintain your previous position, update it based on the AI's reasoning,
  or refine your view -- per your persona's reliance level.
- Be clinically plausible and grounded in the case facts.
- Do NOT invent new findings not present in the case description.

[Termination Decision]
Decide CONTINUE or END. Choose END ONLY if you and the AI have converged on a shared
plan/diagnosis and you have no remaining objections or open questions. Otherwise CONTINUE.

[Style Constraint]
- Keep your response under 5 sentences.
- Focus on clinical evidence.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your message responding to the AI partner's latest message",
  "decision": "CONTINUE or END"
}

Case:
A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

Image Explanation:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showing fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensity involving the periventricular regions, corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of the internal capsule, the external capsule (A) the medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts of the medulla, cerebellar peduncle, and the dentate nuclei (B, circle).

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: My initial assessment is that this is a case of adult-onset leukodystrophy, likely hereditary spastic paraplegia or a related disorder, given the combination of progressive spasticity, cognitive decline, neuropathy, and characteristic white matter changes on MRI with an Ashkenazi Jewish background. The most appropriate next step is to order genetic testing, specifically for *SPG4*, *SPG11*, and *GBA* mutations, to confirm a diagnosis and guide counseling. I want to discuss the case with you, AI, focusing on the differential for leukodystrophies in this demographic.
[AI Assistant]: You've correctly identified an adult-onset leukodystrophy with a strong hereditary suspicion. The Ashkenazi Jewish background indeed raises the probability of certain disorders, but given the constellation of spasticity, cognitive decline, pseudobulbar affect, and the specific periventricular and corticospinal tract white matter involvement, we should broaden the genetic panel to include disorders like *ABCD1* for adrenomyeloneuropathy, which can present similarly, and *C9orf72*, given the cognitive and motor features. Let's discuss which genetic tests have the highest diagnostic yield here.
[Doctor]: I appreciate you broadening the differential, but adrenomyeloneuropathy is unlikely given the normal VLCFA levels already reported in the case. A *C9orf72* repeat expansion is a consideration for the frontotemporal dementia spectrum, but the profound white matter disease and neuropathy point more strongly to a leukodystrophy. I still believe a focused panel for spastic paraplegia genes (*SPG4*, *SPG11*) and *GBA* for Gaucher-related disease is the highest-yield next step, given his ancestry and the specific imaging findings.
[AI Assistant]: You're right to rule out adrenomyeloneuropathy with normal VLCFAs, and *C9orf72* is less fitting given the prominent leukodystrophy. A focused panel for *SPG11* (which often includes neuropathy and cognitive issues) and *GBA* is a strong starting point. We should also consider adding *SPG7* and *SPG5* to the panel, as they can present with complex phenotypes and are relevant to his ancestry.
[Doctor]: I agree that adding SPG7 and SPG5 to the genetic panel is reasonable given their association with complex hereditary spastic paraplegia phenotypes. However, SPG11 remains my top candidate due to its classic presentation with cognitive decline, neuropathy, and thin corpus callosum, which aligns with the diffuse atrophy seen on his spinal cord MRI. The GBA mutation for Gaucher disease type 3 is also a high priority given his Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry and the neurological presentation. I will order a comprehensive HSP gene panel including these targets.
[AI Assistant]: That's a sound plan. A comprehensive HSP panel targeting *SPG11*, *GBA*, *SPG7*, and *SPG5* is the most logical diagnostic step, efficiently covering the high-yield candidates for this clinical and demographic profile. Given the chronic progressive course, confirming a genetic diagnosis will be crucial for prognosis and family counseling.
[Doctor]: I agree, and will proceed with ordering that comprehensive HSP panel. The urgency now is to obtain a definitive genetic diagnosis to inform prognosis, family counseling, and any potential disease-modifying therapies for Gaucher disease if identified.
[AI Assistant]: Agreed. Securing a definitive genetic diagnosis is the priority, as it directly informs management, such as enzyme replacement therapy for Gaucher disease, and provides clarity for the family. Please update me when the panel results return.
[Doctor]: I will order the comprehensive HSP panel as we've agreed. We have a clear, actionable plan and no outstanding clinical disagreements requiring further discussion.
[AI Assistant]: Excellent. That concludes our collaborative discussion for now. I look forward to hearing the results of the genetic panel to confirm the diagnosis and refine the management plan.
[Doctor]: Yes, the plan is set. I'll order the comprehensive genetic panel and we'll reconvene when the results are available to confirm the diagnosis and finalize management.
[AI Assistant]: Perfect. That's a solid diagnostic plan. I'll be available to help interpret the genetic results and discuss the next steps for management and counseling when they arrive.
[Doctor]: Agreed. I'll order the comprehensive HSP panel and will follow up once the results are available.
[AI Assistant]: Perfect. I'm available to help interpret the results and discuss management implications once the genetic panel is completed.
